title: The second paragraph (Deuteronomy 11:13–21)
hook: what we do affects the rain and the harvest

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baruch shem, the whispered line after the Shema. Your line was some words are whispered. What did you say softly? Today, the Shema keeps going, into a paragraph about rain. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

The Shema doesn't stop at its first line, or at the paragraph after it: love the LORD your God with all your heart, teach these words to your children, write them on your doorposts. It has three paragraphs. The second one comes from later in Deuteronomy, and it sounds like a farmer's almanac with a warning label. Rain in its season. Grass for the cattle. And then a hard turn: what the people do reaches the sky and the soil.
screen: `THE SHEMA HAS THREE PARAGRAPHS.` → `A FARMER'S ALMANAC.` → `WITH A WARNING LABEL.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the old Jewish translation: "And it shall come to pass, if ye shall hearken diligently unto My commandments which I command you this day, to love the LORD your God, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." If you do, then rain: "the former rain and the latter rain," grain and wine and oil, grass for your animals. And if your heart turns away to other gods, the sky closes, the land gives no harvest, and you are lost from the good land. Then it repeats the commands from the first paragraph: these words on your heart, on your hand, on your doorposts, taught to your children. Three things stand out. First, the grammar. The first paragraph speaks to you, singular. This one speaks mostly to you, plural. It's about what a whole community does together. Second, the order. The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, explains why this paragraph comes second: first a person accepts the kingdom of heaven, and only then the yoke of the commandments. Third, the phrase serve him with all your heart. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, asks: what is service of the heart? And answers: prayer. The phrase you met a few weeks ago, avodah shebalev, comes from here. The idea that rain answers obedience has troubled readers, and Jewish movements have handled it differently. The classic Reform prayer book left this paragraph out. Orthodox and Conservative prayer books keep it, and newer Reform prayer books often offer it again. Some readers today hear it simply: what we do, together, reaches the land.
screen: `IF YE SHALL HEARKEN DILIGENTLY.` · `YOU, PLURAL: A WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · `THE KINGDOM FIRST, THEN COMMANDMENTS.` · `SERVICE OF THE HEART IS PRAYER.` · then, large: `WHAT WE DO MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: connect one action to its effect. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you did yesterday: a meal you cooked, something you threw away, a word you said in anger or in kindness. Now follow it outward. Where did the food come from, and whose rain grew it? Where did the trash go? Who carried that word home with them? Follow it two or three steps, slowly. Notice how far one small action travels. The bell holds the time.
Avodah shebalev. Service of the heart — the Talmud's name for prayer, drawn from the Shema's second paragraph: serve Him with all your heart.
Your line: what we do matters. Today, choose one action with an effect you'll never see, and do it well anyway. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: The second paragraph of the Shema, Deuteronomy 11:13–21, is said morning and evening after the first; in some Reform prayer books it is optional or replaced, while Orthodox and Conservative prayer books include it.
